reason: Supported by acute-exercise affect meta-analyses; 'most people' and the low-to-moderate intensity case make the during-the-walk part defensible.
Matches the sedentary-break literature and is hedged appropriately.

Unevidenced folklore. 'Stretching overhead wakes up your whole body' has no mechanism and no study behind it; 'wake up your whole body' is not even a checkable claim. If the intended point is that any movement raises alertness, say that instead of attributing it to the overhead stretch.
True and worth saying; dancing is moderate-intensity aerobic activity.

Unsupported superlative. 'More muscles at once than almost any other everyday movement' is a comparative ranking with nothing behind it; stair climbing is demanding but is predominantly lower-body, and carrying, sweeping or swimming recruit at least as much. Either drop the comparison or state what stairs actually do (high effort per minute, legs plus heart).
True; postural muscles and basal metabolism both apply.

Overstated and partly wrong. Collins et al. 2009 (Proc R Soc B) found arm swing cuts the net cost of transport roughly 7-13% at speeds of about 1.0 m/s and above, with no measurable benefit at slow speeds. It lowers the energy cost of a given speed; it does not make you move faster, and the benefit does not apply to a slow stroll. As written it claims both.
Well supported by the postprandial-walking glucose literature, and hedged at the right level for a nine-year-old.

The second clause is garbled — 'unlike a hot drink it works on the way to being useful' does not parse into a claim a reader can evaluate — and it smuggles in an unevidenced comparison against caffeine. The first clause duplicates SF-FCT-000003's territory without adding anything.

Audience mismatch that could cause harm. Thirst is a reliable cue for healthy children and adults, but thirst sensation is blunted with age, and this app is explicitly used by seniors — the group most often advised NOT to wait for thirst. As written it tells exactly the wrong audience to stop paying attention. Needs the age caveat, or should not be stated as a general rule.
Hedged to 'a small workout', which is the correct firmness.
Arithmetic checks out (~70 bpm x 1440 min is about 100,000 beats); fist comparison is standard anatomy.
Satiety-signal delay is well established, and the framing is about noticing fullness rather than restricting food.
True and hedged ('one of the simplest'). Slightly thin on teaching value but it earns its place.
Defensible simplification, though 'vitamins' is loose — much of what varies by color is carotenoids, anthocyanins and other phytochemicals rather than vitamins as such. 'Usually' carries it.
Comparative is a little brisk, but the direction is supported: acute activity lowers state anxiety while rumination sustains it.
Mild dehydration and subjective fatigue are well documented, and the second sentence is encouragement rather than a claim.

'It isn't injury' is stated flatly and is too firm on both counts. DOMS is a symptom of exercise-induced microdamage, and more importantly the sentence is unqualified — it teaches a reader that any post-exercise soreness is benign, which is exactly the belief that gets a real strain walked on. The packet's own SF-FCT-000029 makes the correct distinction; this item contradicts the spirit of it.
Standard, defensible adaptation simplification. Note it overlaps heavily with SF-FCT-000028 and SF-FCT-000030.
'Can help' is the right firmness for active-recovery evidence, which is real but modest and short-lived.
Matches the documented DOMS course (onset ~8-12h, peak ~24-72h).

This is the 'stretching prevents injury' folklore in a new coat. The Cochrane review (Herbert, de Noronha & Kamper 2011, CD004577) pooled 12 studies including a 2,377-participant field trial and found stretching before, after, or both produces no clinically important reduction in post-exercise muscle soreness. Reframing it as 'less tight' rather than 'less sore' does not rescue the claim — there is no evidence for a next-day tightness benefit either. The claim itself is the problem, not the wording.

Teaches nothing. 'Helps your body keep up with everything else you do' names no mechanism, no timeframe and no observable effect, and it is the third near-identical rest-day item in this block (022, 028, 030). A true but empty item is still a failure under the rubric.

'Relax faster' is a comparative with no stated comparator and weak evidence behind it. Systematic reviews of post-exercise heat and warm-water immersion show modest and mixed effects on soreness and recovery, with no clear advantage over passive rest. Also, given a nine-year-old audience, a claim about hot water should not be issued without a temperature caution.

The negation is false. Muscle protein synthesis and the repair/adaptation signalling cascade begin during and immediately after exercise, not only once you stop; 'not while you're still exercising' asserts a hard boundary that does not exist. It is also a near-duplicate of SF-FCT-000022, which makes the same point without the false half.
Genuinely useful safety content, correctly firm.
Motivational filler, not a fact. 'Come back stronger for the next one' restates SF-FCT-000022 and SF-FCT-000026 with no added content and no mechanism a reader learns anything from.

'Most' is an unquantified proportional claim nobody has measured. Tissue repair runs around the clock; what is supported is that some repair-related processes (growth hormone release, elevated protein synthesis) are concentrated in deep sleep. State that instead of a share of the total.
Good — the 'doesn't buy you fewer hours' clause is exactly the kind of honest limit the library needs more of.
Melatonin suppression by evening light is established; 'can trick' is the right firmness given that device-screen effect sizes are debated.

The condition that makes this true is missing. Short naps do not disrupt night sleep when taken in the early afternoon; naps taken late in the day, or long ones, demonstrably do. The item states 'without ruining your night's sleep' flatly while omitting the timing caveat, so a reader who naps at 6pm has been misinformed by it.
Supported by the thermoregulatory sleep-onset literature and hedged to 'most people'.
The sleep-need claim matches AASM/CDC age guidance; 'because their bodies are still growing' is a loose but acceptable child-level reason.

Imprecise as stated. The deep muscle relaxation people mean here is REM atonia, a feature of one sleep stage, not of sleep generally; muscle tone during NREM is not obviously lower than during quiet waking rest. The 'more than almost any other time' superlative is not supported for sleep as a whole, and the item teaches nothing actionable either way.

The dose is invented. Balance-training studies that show improvement use roughly 10-15 minutes of practice three or more times a week over 4-6 weeks; 'a few seconds a day' is far below any studied dose and there is no evidence it produces the promised gain. The activity is fine and safe — the quantity attached to it is not supportable.
Supported by the falls-prevention evidence, and the 'not just for athletes' framing suits the senior audience.
Correct at a child's level: vision, vestibular system, proprioception.

Safety violation — the rubric explicitly bans eyes-closed movement, and this item is an invitation to try it. It tells a nine-year-old or a senior to close their eyes while standing, and the fall risk IS the demonstration, so the danger is the point of the item rather than an incidental side effect. It carries no instruction to hold onto something or sit down. In a falls-aware app aimed partly at older adults this should not ship in any form; the same teaching point is already made safely by SF-FCT-000043.
True and appropriately modest; uneven-surface walking does challenge proprioception and balance. Descriptive, not instructional, so no fall-risk framing needed.
Distributed practice (short, frequent) beating massed practice is supported in motor learning, including balance-board studies spaced across days. 'tends to' keeps the firmness honest.
An asymmetric load genuinely shifts the centre of mass and loads balance; harmless and concrete.
Standard functional-balance example, true and useful.

'the exact same' is stated far more firmly than anything supports, and it is the one item here with a safety edge: balance work for an older adult is normally prescribed with a hand on a chair or counter and fall precautions, which toddler balance play is not. Either soften to 'similar' and name the support, or cut.
True at the level given; a task-level benefit, not an injury-prevention claim.
Frequency-over-volume for range-of-motion gains is consistent with ACSM guidance (stretch most days rather than one weekly session).

Diurnal ROM variation is real (studies find peak flexibility around 16:00, stiffer mornings), and the item correctly flags it as small and meaningless day to day. Good example of matching firmness to evidence.
20-30s matches standard guidance (ACSM 10-30s), and 'time to relax' is a fair simplification of viscoelastic stress relaxation.
True and deliberately non-body-comparing; good framing for a mixed-age audience.
Muscle temperature does increase tissue compliance. Notably it stops short of the 'stretching prevents injury' folklore.
Hedged with 'usually' and pairs the age difference with an encouraging, accurate second clause.
Passive heating improving perceived and measured ROM is supported; the 'can feel easier' hedge keeps it subjective rather than claiming a mechanism it cannot support.
Ankle dorsiflexion ROM is a well-documented contributor to gait and balance, especially in older adults.

States the function of yawning as settled ('is your body's natural way of waking itself up') when it is genuinely unresolved science - brain cooling, arousal and social-contagion hypotheses all compete and none is established. Either reclassify as `contested` and say so in the text, or rewrite to describe what pandiculation feels like rather than asserting its purpose.
Consistent cueing supporting habit recall is well supported.
Directly matches Lally et al. 2010: a single missed opportunity did not materially affect habit formation. True and the right message for a streak app.
Repetition frequency driving automaticity is supported; hedged with 'tend to'.
Friction reduction / environmental cueing; concrete and actionable.
Anchoring a new behaviour to an existing stable cue is the core finding of the habit-formation literature.
The operative advice (substitution beats bare removal) is supported, and the premise is consistent with the finding that old habits are suppressed rather than erased.
Framed as advice with 'usually'; low risk and genuinely actionable.
First clause matches Lally (median 66 days, range 18-254, against the popular 21-day figure). Would be stronger with the number, but nothing here is overstated.
Reinforcement stated at a simplification level a nine-year-old can hold without it becoming wrong.
Parental modelling and child activity are reliably associated; 'more likely' correctly stops short of claiming cause.
No health claim to get wrong; concrete and usable.
True and inclusive across the app's age range.
True, and it frames age difference without ranking bodies.

Not a fact - it asserts a taste preference ('can be just as fun as the sit-down kind') as though it were information, and it teaches the reader nothing they did not already have an opinion about. Replace with something concrete, e.g. a specific active game a mixed-age family can actually play.
Incidental/non-exercise activity counting toward daily movement is well supported.
Modelling outweighing instruction is broadly supported, and 'often' keeps it from being a law.
Harmless, specific, and no claim that needs sourcing.
Learning-by-teaching effect, hedged with 'can'.
Social support improving exercise adherence is supported; 'tend to' is the right firmness.
Accurate: roughly 300 bones at birth fusing to 206 in adults.

The number is roughly double the evidence. Measured maximum molar bite force in healthy adults is about 120-200 lb (roughly 400-800 N), not 'a few hundred pounds'; only rare outliers and Guinness-style records exceed that, and children are well below it. Also note many popular sources quote 120-160 PSI, a pressure, and the item has silently converted it to a force. The contested framing itself is handled well - the text does say nobody agrees how to measure it - so fix the figure (e.g. 'over a hundred pounds') and keep the framing.
True; axial loading compresses the intervertebral discs over the day. 'Gravity squishes you' is a fair simplification, not a misleading one.
Accurate: eight muscles, four intrinsic and four extrinsic.
Deliberately conservative - it avoids both the old '10,000 odours' figure and the disputed '1 trillion' claim. Thousands is safely true.
Well established (cerebellar prediction of self-generated touch cancels the sensation).

The compression comparison is wrong in the reader's direction. Cortical bone is about 150-220 MPa in compression against roughly 20-40 MPa for ordinary structural concrete - bone is several times stronger, and more so per unit weight since it is also lighter, so 'about as well as concrete' understates it and the 'for how light it is' clause makes the comparison ambiguous as to whether it is absolute or per weight. The tension half is fine (bone ~100-130 MPa vs structural steel ~400-550 MPa). Rewrite with one clearly stated basis of comparison.
True and correctly hedged as 'one of the few' - humans are effectively unique in whole-body eccrine sweating, with horses the usual other example by a different mechanism.

The unit is doing all the work and is unstated. About 200 million litres over a lifetime is roughly 80-100 Olympic-size pools, but a nine-year-old reads 'swimming pool' as a backyard pool, where the true figure is several thousand - so the item is off by about 50x for the pool most readers will picture. Say 'Olympic-size swimming pools'.
Standard and accurate simplification of the inverted-pendulum gait model.
Counter-rotating arm swing does offset the angular momentum generated by the legs and pelvis, reducing torso rotation. Correct at this level of detail.

Overstated: 'Going down stairs is what makes your legs ache the next day' names one cause as the cause. Delayed soreness follows unaccustomed eccentric loading generally (downhill walking, lowering weights, new activity of any kind), not stairs specifically. Also near-duplicate of SF-FCT-000130, which states the same mechanism correctly and generally.
Contralateral trunk side-flexors working harder under a one-sided load is sound biomechanics.

Marked 'established', but the cited source contradicts the firmness. Xu & Rhodes, 'Oxygen uptake kinetics during exercise', Sports Medicine 1999 (PMID 10368878) states that TWO COMPETING THEORIES debate whether oxygen delivery capacity or muscle utilization capacity limits the rate of VO2 rise at exercise onset. The item presents the delivery explanation ('your heart and lungs take a couple of minutes to catch up') as settled fact. Either soften to the observed phenomenon (VO2 lags behind demand at onset) or mark the mechanism as contested.

Dangling referent: the item opens with 'That's why' but nothing precedes it. These are served one at a time, so a reader who does not get SF-FCT-000110 immediately before it is being told 'that's why' about nothing. Needs to be self-contained (state the evaporation mechanism, then the humidity consequence) or merged into SF-FCT-000110.

Factually wrong as written. 'Your lungs contain no muscle of their own' is false: the lungs contain airway (bronchial) smooth muscle throughout the bronchial tree down to the terminal bronchioles, plus vascular smooth muscle. Airway smooth muscle is precisely what contracts in an asthma attack, so this is not a harmless simplification for a 9-year-old audience. The true claim is that the lungs contain no SKELETAL muscle and cannot move air by themselves - the diaphragm and intercostals do that.
Haem/heme as an iron-bearing porphyrin ring is correct. Note the British spelling 'haem' is inconsistent with the rest of the library's US spelling.

The stated mechanism misleads. 'Your stomach has no teeth' implies the stomach does no mechanical breakdown, but the gastric antrum grinds food by muscular contraction until particles are small enough to pass the pylorus - mechanical breakdown is a large part of what the stomach does. The benefit claim ('makes everything after it easier') is also broader and firmer than the evidence, which is mostly small studies on bolus particle size, gastric emptying and satiety, not a general digestive benefit. This reads as the familiar chew-your-food folklore.

'One of the very few body reactions nobody can do on purpose' is false. Nearly every autonomic response is involuntary in exactly the same way: pupil dilation, goosebumps, sweating, gut motility, heart rate. Blushing is unremarkable in this respect, so the claim that makes the item interesting is the part that is wrong. The first half (facial vasodilation) is fine.
Red cell lifespan is about 120 days, so 'not more than a few months old' holds.

Fails the quality bar: a bare list with no explanation, no mechanism and nothing a reader learns beyond naming umami 'savory'. It also states 'there are five basic tastes' as settled, when fat (oleogustus) is an actively argued candidate sixth - if the item is kept at this confidence it should not be phrased as a closed count. Needs an actual idea attached (e.g. why bitter detection exists) to earn a slot.

The reasoning is a non-sequitur: a drink feeling good before you consciously wanted one is not evidence that thirst lags your fluid state. The item is also vague about what thirst supposedly lags behind, and in that vagueness it points at the contested 'if you're thirsty it's already too late / drink ahead of thirst' advice, which is not the current consensus for ordinary activity. Either state the specific, supportable version (thirst is often satisfied before rehydration is complete, and during hard sweating people typically under-drink) or cut it.
Repeated bout effect, well established.

States a mechanism more firmly than the evidence supports. Light movement does raise blood flow, but 'which is why a gentle walk often feels better than lying down' asserts blood flow as the cause of the relief. Active recovery's effect on delayed soreness is modest and short-lived in the literature, and its mechanism is not settled. Drop the causal 'which is why', or present the walk as something people report rather than something blood flow explains.
Overlaps SF-FCT-000135; consider whether both are needed.

Internally contradictory. It opens 'isn't paying anything back', then describes the body putting fuel stores back where they belong - which is, in plain English, paying something back. The point being aimed at (that post-exercise oxygen use is not a lactate 'oxygen debt') is worth making, but as written the reader is told the opposite of the sentence that follows.
Tendon and ligament hypovascularity relative to muscle is standard.
Cold slowing sensory nerve conduction is a well-supported analgesia mechanism, and 'largely' is appropriately hedged.
Consistent with detraining literature; timescale claim is correct.
Standard talk test, stated at the right level of firmness.
The largest GH pulse does occur with the first slow-wave sleep episode; GH's role in tissue repair is standard physiology.
Synovial fluid thixotropy is the mainstream explanation; 'within a minute' is slightly tighter than sources say ('a few minutes') but not misleading.

The stated mechanism is wrong. Stopping abruptly does not make heart rate 'drop off a cliff' — heart rate falls gradually either way (that is what HR recovery measures). The real effect of an abrupt stop is blood pooling in the legs and a drop in blood pressure, which is what causes the light-headedness. Rewrite around blood pooling, or drop the 'cliff' framing; as written it teaches a mechanism that does not exist.
Low information density and overlaps SF-FCT-000139/149, but nothing false or unsafe.
Specificity of adaptation plus plateau; fair as a simplification.
Muscle protein synthesis stays elevated for 24-48h after exercise; no diet prescription attached.
Morning/post-stillness stiffness is a real and commonly reported pattern; heavy overlap with SF-FCT-000142 though.

This is the classic supercompensation curve stated as a mechanical certainty for every hard session ('the repair overshoots slightly, and you come back a little stronger than before'). Supercompensation is a contested training model, not an established per-session physiological event — different systems recover at different rates and single-session overshoot in performance has not been reliably demonstrated. Either soften to 'over weeks of hard efforts and recovery you end up stronger' or re-tag as contested and say so in the text.
Matches detraining evidence for a one-week layoff.
Caffeine is an adenosine receptor antagonist; the framing is accurate and useful.
REM atonia, correctly described.
Homeostatic sleep pressure; the tank analogy does not overreach.
Core temperature begins falling roughly two hours before habitual sleep onset.
Morning light is the dominant zeitgeber; correctly stated.
Chronotype is partly heritable and shifts with age; the non-judgemental framing is right for the audience.
Pubertal circadian phase delay is well documented.
Hedged to 'most' rather than the usual unsourced '95%' figure.

The mechanism is right but the word 'simply' makes a blanket reassurance out of it. Habitual loud snoring is the cardinal symptom of obstructive sleep apnea — roughly 2-3% of children and a far higher share of older adults — and this item, aimed at 9-year-olds and seniors, tells the reader snoring is nothing but a noise. Remove 'simply' and add a non-diagnostic clause (e.g. that loud, habitual snoring or pauses in breathing are worth mentioning to a doctor).
Ordinary room-level light suppresses and delays melatonin in most people; 'can' keeps it appropriately hedged.
Social jetlag, correctly described.
Sleep inertia is worse on waking from slow-wave sleep; accurate.
Distal heat loss and sleep onset; the 'slightly cool room' guidance is not overstated.

Hedged with 'tends to', and the light-emitting-eReader vs paper comparison supports both named mechanisms. Note the sleep-onset effect is modest (~10 minutes), so the text must not be firmed up in editing.
REM is concentrated in the later cycles, so a short night cuts REM disproportionately.

Stated far more firmly than the evidence supports, and partly contradicted. Skin does not repair faster while you sleep: Hoyle et al. (Science Translational Medicine, 2017) found human burns sustained at night healed about 60% slower than daytime burns, because fibroblast mobilisation is circadian and peaks in the active phase. Overnight muscle protein synthesis is limited by amino acid availability rather than elevated by sleep per se, and bone resorption markers actually peak overnight. What is defensible is that poor or short sleep impairs repair — that is the claim to make, not a blanket 'skin, muscle and bone all repair faster while you're asleep'.
Brief arousals are normal and usually unremembered; reassuring without being medical advice.
Semicircular canals, correctly described for rotation; omitting the otoliths is a fair simplification.
Endolymph inertia and cupula deflection; accurate.
Vision, vestibular and somatosensory integration; the 'vote' framing teaches the idea well.
Sensory conflict is the standard explanation used by major health bodies.
Ankle and hip postural strategies are established in the postural-control literature.
Visual fixation measurably improves postural stability.
Correct physics: a long pole raises rotational inertia, slowing the rate of tip.
Spotting is correctly described; 'avoid' is slightly absolute (dancers also habituate vestibularly) but not misleading.
Proprioception, correctly named. The eyes-shut example is a seated finger-to-nose illustration, not an eyes-closed movement instruction, so it does not trip the safety rule.
Base-of-support size and stability; correct and no instruction to attempt anything risky.

Misattributes the cat righting reflex to a 'faster' inner ear. The vestibular system only triggers the reflex — humans have that part too and it is not the limiting factor. What lets a cat land on its feet is body mechanics: an unusually flexible spine and no functional collarbone, letting it counter-rotate front and back halves and reorient while conserving angular momentum. As written it teaches the wrong cause.
Whole-body centre of mass sits roughly at navel level (anterior to S2); 'roughly' carries the approximation honestly.
Recycled public-domain joke-book staple ('two-tired'); instantly recognizable and not original to StreakFit.
Punchline substitutes a word without creating a double meaning: 'spill the iron' is not a phrase and iron does not spill. The kettlebell/iron link is there but the idiom swap does no comic work.
Clean double meaning on 'skipped' (rope-skipping / being passed over); original and warm.
Rests on the adult idiom 'that's a reach' (exaggerating), which a nine-year-old is unlikely to have. The obvious child-legible pun, 'stretch the truth', is sitting right there unused.
Generic schoolyard pun that reads as stock; the stress also does not match ('gee-OG-raphy' vs 'JOG-raphy'), so the pun is a beat off when read aloud.
Broken construction: the setup asks for a vegetable and the punchline is a buffet, which is not a vegetable. 'Buffet' is also said 'buh-FAY', so the 'buff' pun does not survive being read aloud.
No twist: the punchline just restates 'smoothie' as 'smooth'. Nothing flips meaning, and 'blush' gives the reward line an odd romantic framing for a nine-year-old.
Phonetically clean ('en-thusiast' / 'hen-thusiast'), gettable, no target but the chicken.
Bench press / branch press lands in one beat and is age-legible.
Real double meaning on 'leaf'; mild but sound and warm.
Factual mismatch breaks the pun: broccoli has florets, not sprouts. The joke wants a Brussels sprout, or the vegetable needs changing.
'Well-rounded' carries both the shape and the training sense; the leg-day framing stays about the orange, not about anyone's body.
No joke mechanism at all: 'the backstroke' is a literal, expected answer for a fish. Setup and punchline are the same thought with no twist or wordplay.
'Stepped up' works in both senses; short, sound, quietly charming.
Punchline is a bland positive statement with no wordplay or twist. 'Cool as a cucumber' is a worn idiom and the line never even completes it.
'Egg-cited' is a tired staple, and the setup does not set it up: jogging has no connection to excitement, so the two halves are unrelated.
'Support' genuinely means two things here; gentle and in voice. 'Wellness club' is slightly stiff phrasing but works.
The pun never lands on the page: 'dog-a practitioner' needs the reader to supply 'yoga', and the word 'yoga' already appears in the setup, so the joke is just the word restated with a hyphen.
Recycled public-domain joke ('outstanding in his field', normally the scarecrow or the corn) with the fruit swapped in. Recognizable to almost every adult reader.
Salad dressing / dressing the part is a real double meaning, and the theatre setup is a fresh frame for it.
'Un-be-leaf-able' is a widely circulated stock pun, and nothing about a workout makes plants say it: the setup and punchline are unconnected.
No twist: frogs jump, so 'jumping jacks' is the literal expected answer, not a punchline. Also one of the most-told kids' joke staples.
Raisin / raising is clean and gettable, and setting the bar too high is an idea this app's readers will recognize in themselves.
Boulder / bolder lands cleanly; the rest-to-bold link is loose but readable.

A mangled version of the famous 'it saw the salad dressing' joke: the original pun has been removed and replaced with jealousy over attention, which is both unfunny and a comparison between two characters rather than a wordplay.
Zest / best works in one beat and is age-legible.
'Souper' is one of the most worn puns in circulation, and 'souper fit' is not a phrase the pun transforms; there is no second meaning, only a respelling.

Leans on the single most famous mushroom joke ('a fun guy') but never lands it: the punchline says 'fungi' and then explains relaxation in plain words, so the reader does all the work and gets a joke they already know.
'Rose to the occasion' is familiar but genuinely double-meaning here, and the pride framing is on-voice.
Near-duplicate of SF-JOK-000014, which already uses 'stepped up'. 'A steeped-up workout buddy' is also not an idiom, so the pun has nothing to bounce off.
Not a joke: the punchline is a bland positive statement ('well-watered and blooming') with no wordplay, twist or surprise of any kind.
No punchline: 'slow and steady stretching' is the literal expected answer for a turtle, and 'slow and steady' is a stock phrase used straight.
The 'kneaded/needed' pun is never activated, so the line reads as a literal baking description; it also repeats the bread subject already used in SF-JOK-000029.
The strongest item in the packet: in character, self-deprecating, original, and the humour is entirely at the raccoon's expense.
Not a joke: a bland positive description of a cactus with no twist. 'Well-grounded' is also reused verbatim in SF-JOK-000044.
No wordplay and no surprise: 'nice and slow' is the literal expected answer for a snail. Near-identical in shape and idea to SF-JOK-000032.
Not a joke at all: a bland affirmation with no setup-payoff relationship. Occupies a reader's one reward slot for the day and gives nothing back.
The construction is fine but 'peeling good' is an extremely well-worn staple that most readers will have met already; needs a fresher turn on the banana.
Two faults: there is no pun, only a literal description; and the setup judges by how something 'looks so fit', which is exactly the appearance framing this content must avoid.
Not a joke: 'a step in the right direction' is a motivational cliche delivered straight, with no second meaning beyond the one everybody already uses.
The punchline rewards skipping the workout, which is the wrong message on a completion screen, and the available pun ('full of hot air') is never actually made.
The board/bored pun produces a phrase that means nothing: being 'bored with stress' is not a thing, and a wave is not a board, so the substitution has no anchor.
The pun does not exist: clocks have hands, not joints, so 'keep good time with its joints' joins a clock idiom to a body part the clock does not have. A non-sequitur in a joke's shape.
No wordplay, just adjectives ('well-grounded and crunchy strong', which is not even grammatical), and 'well-grounded' duplicates SF-JOK-000035.
Non-sequitur: a map has nothing to do with 'the long way to feeling great', and the punchline is a bland positive sentiment rather than a twist.
