Sensorimotor adaptation to ship motion and the readaptation on land are well described; the claim is hedged at the right level and teaches a real mechanism.

"in a way standing still never can" is an absolute nobody measured, and the underlying claim that carrying a tray trains balance is asserted, not evidenced. Drop the absolute and state it as a plausible difference in demand, not a training effect.

Safety: a single-leg stand at a bathroom sink, on a hard and often wet floor, is suggested to an audience that includes seniors, with no mention of keeping a hand near the counter and no naming of the fall risk. Also frames it as "two minutes of practice" when nobody balances on one foot for the full two minutes.
Postural control continues maturing well past toddlerhood into adolescence. True, correctly unquantified, and useful for a young reader.
Symmetric loading keeps the centre of mass closer to the base of support; a one-sided load forces trunk compensation. True at this level of detail, no overclaim.
Plantar cutaneous feedback is a genuine contributor to postural control, and the item hedges honestly ("part of why", "feels steadier") rather than claiming barefoot is measurably better.
Age-related decline in balance is well established; the second clause is an explicit value judgement about spending a minute, not a dose or sufficiency claim.
Single-support phase of gait is real and this reframes something familiar without overstating it.

Firmness. "Most of the tightness" is a proportion nobody measured, and the mechanism is actively argued: current reviews find both reduced passive stiffness and increased stretch tolerance contribute, with tolerance dominant only over longer training periods. Either hedge ("a lot of what you feel is...") or mark contested and say the question is open.

Two defects. It opens with "That's why", a dangling referent to SF-FCT-000190 that breaks when the item is served on its own, which is how this library is read. And "your body has decided the position is safe" is a vivid causal mechanism stated as fact for an acute effect whose cause is not settled.
Hamstrings are biarticular and hip/knee position genuinely changes what a forward bend loads. Accurate and explanatory.

"a lot of why" is an unmeasured proportion, and "shortened position" is the weakest-supported version of this claim. Evidence supports increased passive hip-flexor stiffness and reduced hip extension after prolonged sitting, not structural shortening; no study links length of sitting to hip flexor tightness directly. Rewrite as stiffness, and drop the proportion.
Correct contrast between a multiaxial and a uniaxial joint, and the "on purpose" framing teaches the trade-off rather than just naming parts.
The glenohumeral joint being the most mobile joint in the body is standard anatomy, and the mobility/stability trade-off is correctly stated.

Both halves are wrong in a safety-relevant direction. Ballistic stretching is discouraged primarily for injury risk, not merely because it is "less controlled", and the item explicitly downplays that. And "the range you gain looks much the same either way" is contradicted: meta-analytic comparisons put ballistic stretching's effect on range of motion below static and PNF. Telling a nine-year-old that bouncing gets the same result is the opposite of the guideline.
Individual variation in connective tissue and joint laxity is real, and "some people" keeps it appropriately unquantified. Also usefully defuses comparison between bodies.

The exhale-lets-you-sink-further claim is gym folklore stated as fact ("usually"), with no good evidence behind it, and "Holding your breath does the opposite" invents a matching effect. It also introduces breath-holding as a technique to a nine-year-old audience, which the safety rules avoid. Cut the breath-holding half or reframe the whole item as relaxation, not range.
This is the mainstream warm-up recommendation (ACSM and reviews of acute stretching effects): dynamic movement before activity, static afterwards. The comparative is earned.
Distinguishing stretch tension from sharp pain is exactly the right safety cue for this audience, and it is stated without diagnosing anything.
Accurate description of segmental spinal motion summing to gross range. Teaches something a reader will not have pictured.
Verified: the Achilles is described in the anatomical literature as the thickest and strongest tendon in the body, formed from gastrocnemius and soleus and inserting on the calcaneus.
Pandiculation is a real, widely observed vertebrate behaviour and naming it is worth the reader's attention. The "old enough to have its own name" line is a loose flourish but makes no health claim.
Latissimus dorsi runs from the humerus to the thoracolumbar fascia and lower spine, so an overhead reach does load far more than the arm. Accurate.
Accurate description of psoas major, correctly left unnamed for a nine-year-old, and the length of the muscle is genuinely surprising.

"almost nothing" is an overstatement and it contradicts SF-FCT-000197 in this same packet: generalised connective-tissue laxity is precisely why hypermobility is scored across multiple joints. Joint specificity is real; the strength of the claim is not. Soften to "tell you less than you would think".

"the same mechanism" is an unearned identity claim between two practices that have not been shown to work identically, and what follows the colon is a description of practice (regular time at end range), not a mechanism. Restate as "work the same way in practice" or cut the mechanism framing.

Quality failure. It restates SF-FCT-000203 with the content removed and teaches nothing checkable; "one your body asked for on its own" is a phrase, not a fact. Either fold into the pandiculation item or give it real content.

Anatomically wrong: the ankle (talocrural) joint is classified as a uniaxial hinge, the same category as the knee and elbow; the side-to-side motion comes from the subtalar joint below it. "universal joints" is also not a standard classification for the wrist, which is condyloid. And "can't possibly suit all of them" is an overclaim on top of the error.

Stated more firmly than the neuroscience supports. The clean prefrontal-to-striatum handoff is the old account; current work finds both systems remain active and compete rather than one replacing the other, and cortical involvement is task-dependent. "stops needing willpower" also overstates automaticity. Should be hedged or marked contested.

Two proportions nobody measured: "nearly always" and "Most people feel better a few minutes in". There is real work on people mispredicting how exercise will feel, but not at this firmness. Label editorial or hedge to "often".

An absolute and a superlative in one sentence. "Every habit needs a cue" is stated as a law, and "the most reliable cue is" ranks cue types against each other on no measurement — existing-routine anchoring is supported as effective, not as most reliable.
Implementation intentions are among the better-replicated findings in this area, and "noticeably more likely" is hedged correctly rather than quoting an effect size the item cannot source.

"beats" is a head-to-head comparative between two approaches that have not been compared head to head. It is also advice, not a simplified fact, so the confidence label is wrong — SF-FCT-000220 shows `editorial` is available and unused here.

Misstates the peak-end rule: it is peak AND end that dominate retrospective evaluation, and this item drops the peak entirely. "is what pulls you back" then asserts a single cause for return behaviour that the evidence supports only as one predictor among several.

"far more" is an unmeasured comparative. The defensible version — missing a single day does not derail habit formation — is worth saying, but not with a magnitude attached, and this is editorial rather than simplified.

"Streaks work because" asserts a mechanism for the app's own core feature with nothing behind it, and picks one explanation (visibility) over the more obvious ones (loss aversion, commitment). Either hedge to "part of why streaks work" or mark it editorial and own it as a product opinion.

The reactivity of self-monitoring is a real effect, but "purely because you're now paying attention to it" is a mechanism overclaim — tracking also changes what people choose to do because they know it will be recorded. Drop "purely".

"usually physical" is an unmeasured proportion and is likely wrong: the barriers people report most are time, fatigue and how they expect it to feel, not where the shoes are. The examples are good; the ranking claim is not earned.

Honestly labelled `editorial`, which is the right call for a claim like this, and it is safe, plausible and consistent with work on accountability and commitment. The only item in the packet whose confidence field is doing real work.
"holds up better" is presented as a finding but is a comparative nobody measured. Cue consistency is supported in general; time-of-day versus mood specifically is not. Hedge or relabel editorial.
Plainly advice in advice voice, sound, safe, and consistent with the implementation-intention literature without claiming to be a measurement.
Reward immediacy is a well-supported principle of learning, and "stick best" here refers to a genuine and large timing effect rather than an invented ranking.

"The clearest sign" is an unearned superlative. Reduced conscious deliberation and a sense of oddity when skipping are indicators of automaticity, but nothing establishes this as the clearest one. "A good sign" fixes it.
A clean, safe framing that moves attention from outcome goals to today's action, with no empirical claim to overstate.
"faster than changing your mind does" is a speed comparison between two things never measured against each other. The environment-shapes-behaviour point survives without the race.

Planning fallacy, correctly stated including the direction of the error (people overestimate what they will finish). Hedged with 'reliably poor' rather than a made-up percentage. Age-appropriate and useful.

Small-dose habit framing is consistent with the app's values and safe; the second clause (repetition ingrains whatever pattern is repeated) is ordinary motor-learning and is stated without a fake number. Teaches something real about form.

Firmness defect. 'is what keeps MOST streaks alive' is an unearned proportion — nobody measured what keeps most streaks alive. The underlying idea (implementation intentions / if-then plans help adherence) is supported, but it is stated as a measured majority. Soften to something like 'Deciding in advance what you'll do on the day you don't feel like it is one of the things that keeps a streak alive.'

Two unearned comparatives in one item: 'Kids move most when nobody calls it exercise' (superlative) and 'tends to go on considerably longer' (a quantified duration comparison nobody measured here). The core observation — framing activity as play rather than exercise raises engagement — is plausible but is stated far more firmly than any cited evidence. Also `simplified` with no source for what is really a behavioural research claim.
Hedged ('most children', 'given time, space, and no instructions'), safe, and true of free play at the level of detail given. The closing line is editorial colour rather than a factual overreach.
Properly hedged with 'often'. Side-by-side walking reducing the pressure of a hard conversation is a modest, non-medical claim and is not stated as a measured effect. Safe for all ages.
Household behaviour concordance is real and the item hedges twice ('usually', 'a little'). No mechanism is invented and no proportion is claimed.
Sibling modelling is well documented, and the claim is hedged with 'tend to'. The 'coaches' line is framing, not an invented effect. Safe and age-appropriate.

Stated as a guaranteed outcome: a weekly repeat 'turns it into a landmark that kids still remember years later.' Family-ritual research supports that rituals are valued and remembered, but not that repeating anything weekly reliably produces a decades-long memory. Needs a hedge ('can become', 'often') rather than a promise.
'far more likely' is an unearned magnitude. Choice/autonomy does support intrinsic motivation, but the size of the effect here is invented. Drop 'far' or cite the autonomy-support evidence.
Straightforwardly true (incidental daily activity is real movement), no number claimed, safe, and it usefully reframes existing activity without any body or weight framing.

Safety. The item invites a nine-year-old to race 'to the end of the street' and does not name the traffic hazard, which the rubric requires for anything a child could copy and be hurt by. Relocate it to a safe setting (park, yard, path) or name the condition explicitly.
Warm, safe, non-comparative, and makes a genuine point about modelling across generations. No factual claim to overreach on.
True at the level given and directly aligned with the app's no-comparison stance. States a direction, not a measured effect size.
True, safe, and it reframes chores as movement without any weight or body-composition framing. Modest but it does teach the reframe.

Hedged with 'usually' and framed against adult expectation rather than as a measurement. Children being more fatigue-resistant in intermittent play is well supported, and the boredom half is plainly observational.
Inclusive, safe, no comparison of bodies, and it makes a real point about pacing a group. Nothing to verify and nothing overstated.

'one of the few things' is an unearned superlative and is easy to falsify — a nine-year-old and a sixty-year-old can genuinely cook, play games, garden or make music side by side too. The point survives without the ranking: say movement is one of the things they can do side by side at their own speeds.
Hedged with 'often', and the accountability/telling-someone effect is a reasonable, non-medical claim. No proportion or magnitude invented.

Three firmness problems stacked: 'the MOST reliable exercise partners', 'in MOST households', and the causal 'mainly because'. None of that is measured, and the dog-walking literature is actually mixed — a large share of dog owners do not walk their dog regularly. Rewrite as an observation about the daily prompt a dog provides, without the superlative or the household proportion.
True and non-quantified: playground play does develop balance, coordination and confidence. Safe, and the closing point (it doesn't feel like training) is the actual insight.
Correctly labelled `editorial`, which licenses the firmness of 'is the one that sticks'. Safe, no medical claim, and it says something worth reading to an adult user.
Hedged with 'tend to' on both halves and framed as a comparison against adults' own expectations rather than a measured quantity. Consistent with modelling research.

Verified anatomy: the fingers contain no muscle bellies; flexion and extension come from extrinsic forearm muscles acting through long tendons. The puppet-string image is an accurate simplification, not an invented mechanism.
Verified: 26 bones per foot, 52 of roughly 206 bones, which is genuinely about a quarter. The proportion is one of the few in this packet that is actually arithmetic rather than assertion.
Verified: the malleus, incus and stapes are the smallest bones in the body, the largest about 8 mm. 'All three on a fingernail' is a fair size image, not an invented measurement.

Verified: the femur is the longest and strongest bone, and its anterior bow (a real, named feature) is correctly described as a slight curve rather than straight. Good detail that most readers won't know.

Verified on both halves: the function of yawning genuinely is unresolved (and the item says so, which is the honest handling of an open question), and reading or thinking about yawning is a documented contagion trigger. 'Often' is the right hedge.
'More than six hundred' matches the standard skeletal-muscle count and is loose in the safe direction. 'Dozens at once' for a sit-to-stand is qualitative, not a fabricated number.
Microsaccades and fixational drift are established and the item claims nothing beyond their existence and imperceptibility. Genuinely surprising to a reader, which is what this category is for.

Verified: two lobes on the left, three on the right, and the left lung's cardiac notch really is the heart occupying that space. The 'gave up a lobe's worth of space' phrasing is a simplification of standard anatomy, not an invented mechanism.

'About a minute' is the mainstream resting figure (roughly 5 L blood over roughly 5 L/min cardiac output); published estimates run 20-60 seconds, so 'about a minute' is within range and appropriately approximate.

'Tens of thousands of miles' is the correctly loose version of the commonly cited 60,000-mile estimate — notably, the item did NOT commit to the precise figure, which is the right call given the estimate's softness.

True for the motor pathway the item names: myelinated alpha motor fibres conduct at roughly 70-120 m/s, well above highway speed. The comparison is qualitative and correctly scoped to brain-to-muscle signals rather than all nerves.
Established bone biology — vascularised, innervated, continuously remodelled — stated without any dose, rate or proportion. Corrects a real misconception children hold.
Verified: the auricular muscles are present in everyone and voluntary control is variable. Stated with the correct hedge ('only some people'), no proportion invented.
Verified and non-obvious: the visible lingual papillae are not themselves taste buds; the buds sit in the epithelium along the papillae's walls. A genuine correction of a common misconception.

Retronasal olfaction dominating flavour perception is well established in sensory science, and the blocked-nose observation is the everyday evidence for it. The proportion here ('most of the work') is one of the rare ones in this packet that the literature actually supports.
'About a fifth' matches the standard ~20% of resting metabolic rate for the brain, and the 'even when sitting still' clause is the correct and interesting part.

Verified against NASA: spinal lengthening in microgravity is commonly cited as up to about 3%, roughly two inches for a tall adult, so 'an inch or two' is accurate. The item also actively corrects the 'no gravity in space' misconception with the right explanation (free fall), which is a bonus rather than a defect.

Firmness defect of exactly the type this library has. The first half (fingernails grow faster than toenails) is solidly established; the second half — 'the nails on your dominant hand grow fastest of all' — is stated flatly as fact when the evidence is mixed: it rests largely on Bean's decades-long self-observation, and at least one peer-reviewed comparison found no significant right/left difference. Either drop the dominant-hand clause or mark it as something people have noticed but not settled.
Safe, non-clinical resilience framing that explicitly refuses to tell a reader they shouldn't find hard things hard. No mechanism, dose or proportion claimed.

'the one that changes the most' is an unearned superlative, ranking sleep above every other self-care behaviour with nothing to support the ranking. Sleep's importance is not in doubt; the league table is. Rewrite without the ranking, e.g. 'and one of the ones that changes the most.'
Safe, age-appropriate conflict guidance with no medical or psychological claim beyond common sense. Nothing to overstate.

Defines gratitude honestly and explicitly rules out toxic positivity ('isn't pretending things are fine'), which is the right handling for a young audience. No claim about outcomes or benefits, so nothing to overreach.
Editorial, correctly labelled, safe, non-shaming, and useful to a 9-year-old. No factual claim to overstate.
Correctly hedged ('is linked to'), and 'short counts' is supported by the physical-activity/mood literature. Simplified label is honest here.

'Most people are far harsher with themselves than they would ever be out loud' states a measured-sounding proportion and comparative that nobody has measured. The advice is fine; soften to 'many people' or drop the quantifier.

Quasi-medical reassurance: days of tiredness plus irritability is a symptom pattern with many causes (illness, low mood, poor sleep, anaemia), and 'usually a request for rest' is a firmness claim with no source, aimed at 9-year-olds. Either reframe as 'often worth treating as a rest signal' plus 'if it keeps going, tell someone', or drop it.
Qualitative, safe, consistent with validation/emotion-regulation research, and appropriate at min_age 9.

Mislabelled: this is an editorial stance on boundaries, not a 'simplified' factual claim with detail left out. Also 'It doesn't need a reason attached to it' is delivered unqualified to a nine-year-old, where it can read as licence to refuse a caregiver without explanation. Relabel editorial and add the relationship context.
Self-aware hedging ('works more often than it should') keeps the firmness honest, and going outside is safe. Note it overlaps heavily with SF-FCT-000287.
Editorial, correctly labelled, safe, and on-message without claiming anything measurable.
Essentially definitional (responding vs reacting) and safe; the 'simplified' label is loose but the statement does not overreach.
Editorial, correctly labelled, safe, and a genuine idea rather than a platitude.
Safe, non-commercial, no meal-skipping or body-composition framing, and it teaches something real about what self-care actually is.

Social comparison being automatic is well supported, and the item does not shame the reader for it. 'Noticing it is what lets you put it down' is a slightly firm mechanism but stays within simplified.
Editorial and correctly labelled; the comparative is qualitative, not a fabricated measurement, and the advice is safe.

'at any age, in any season, and it doesn't take long' is an unearned universal. The nature-exposure evidence is mostly temperate-season adult samples with modest effects; drop the 'any age, any season' absolutism. Also near-duplicates SF-FCT-000280.

Test craft: guessable without knowing the fact. 'Two seconds', 'At least five minutes on each muscle' and the bare dismissal 'How long you hold it makes no difference' are all non-starters, leaving one survivable option. The explanation's content is fine (20-30s matches ACSM; equal cumulative duration in shorter holds does give similar ROM gains), but 'long enough for the muscle to stop resisting and settle' implies viscoelastic creep when the accepted mechanism is increased stretch tolerance. Needs three plausible durations.

DOMS answer is correct at the simplified level, the lactic-acid distractor is the genuine folk belief rather than a joke, and the clearance timing (~an hour) is right. Safety caveat about persistent sharp pain is present. Correct option is marginally the longest, but the distractors carry real pull.
Cooler room and the core-temperature-drop mechanism are correct, the correct option is the shortest rather than the longest, and all three distractors are plausible sleep-hygiene beliefs.
Correct, and the safety framing (next to a wall or worktop) is in the explanation rather than assumed. Explanation gives a real mechanism (ankle, vision, vestibular) instead of restating the answer.

Core answer (working muscle takes up glucose) and 'ten minutes is enough' are both correct. But the explanation's rebuttal is overstated: 'walking doesn't steal blood from digestion: that's the opposite of what happens' is only true at light intensity — exercise after a meal does reduce splanchnic vascular conductance, substantially so as intensity rises. Reword to 'a gentle walk isn't hard enough to do that' rather than asserting the opposite.
Cue-anchoring is well supported, the distractors are all real instincts people actually have, and the explanation adds a mechanism plus a concrete example rather than restating the option.
True, age-appropriate, and the correct option is the shortest. Distractors are a little easy (walnut, folded newspaper) but the item earns its place on the 100,000-beats detail.

Consistent with the habit-formation evidence that a single missed opportunity does not meaningfully affect habit strength, and the framing is non-punitive. Option 'The streak matters more than the habit underneath it' is a slightly awkward fit for a 'what happens' question but remains a plausible pick.
Correct, mechanically explained, and the distractors (calves only; smaller range; gentler because slower) are all things people genuinely believe.

The answer key is contradicted by the evidence it leans on. Meta-analysis puts parental modelling at a weak association with child activity (summary r about .16) while parental support and encouragement is moderate (about .38) — i.e. the option marked wrong ('being told regularly that exercise matters') is, if anything, the better-supported one. 'Children copy what adults do far more reliably than they follow what they're told' is an unearned comparative pointing the wrong way. Also duplicates SF-TRV-000025.

Two problems. Safety: 'Practicing only with your eyes shut' is offered as a distractor to an audience including seniors, and neither the question nor the explanation names eyes-closed balance work as a fall risk — a wrong answer that a reader may still try. Firmness: 'rehearsal likes frequency more than duration' is a comparative presented as settled; frequency-vs-duration for balance training has not been cleanly separated.

Content is good (specific compressive strength vs overall strength is the right debunk). Test craft fails: the correct option is the longest, the only nuanced one, and the only one not phrased as an absolute — and two distractors are the same sentence with 'stronger'/'weaker' swapped, so a reader who knows nothing picks the hedged one by reflex. Rebuild the distractors.

10-20 minute nap guidance and the sleep-inertia explanation are correct, the correct option is not the longest, and the distractors are all real beliefs. 'Without much cost to that night' is doing a little work unqualified but stays inside simplified for a short nap.
Safe and correct: normal soreness distinguished from warning signs, with a clear stop-and-get-it-looked-at instruction. Options are near-equal in length. Overlaps SF-TRV-000034 in content.

Correct (respiratory sinus arrhythmia is the right mechanism for the long exhale), and it explicitly names the breath-holding danger including in water rather than leaving it as a silent wrong answer. Best-constructed item in the packet.

'Reliably takes some of the heat out of it' is stated more firmly than the evidence supports. Affect labelling has mixed results, unclear mechanisms, and findings that it can interfere with subsequent reappraisal; short-term effects are often null. This is closer to contested than simplified, and the text does not say the question is open. Soften to 'often' and drop 'reliably'.

The correct option is phenomenological (writing forces sequence) rather than an efficacy claim, and the explanation explicitly refuses to claim it solves anything. Correct option is the longest, which is a mild tell, but the distractors are genuine beliefs about journalling.

Definitional rather than an efficacy claim, which is the right call given how contested growth-mindset intervention effects are. The explanation actively heads off the 'you can be anything' inflation, and the correct option is the shortest.
Arousal-reappraisal framing is well supported, safe, and genuinely useful at min_age 9. Distractors are the beliefs a nervous child actually holds.
Vigilance decrement is well established, including that it occurs within tens of minutes and independently of felt tiredness, and brief-break restoration is reasonable at simplified level.

Unearned ranking: 'Enjoyment predicts whether someone is still moving years later better than talent, early starts or encouragement do' is a head-to-head comparison nobody has run, and the encouragement leg is doubtful — parental support/encouragement shows a moderate association with child activity in meta-analysis. Keep the enjoyment claim, drop the league table.

Safe, on-message, and the explanation does real work (comparison changes the subject from 'did I move' to 'am I winning'). 'It works on everyone' is a small over-reach but the claim is a values statement, not a measurement.

The question demands a proportion nobody has measured, and the answer it awards ('Most of it') points against the evidence: parental modelling is weakly associated with child activity (about r .16) while parental support and instruction is moderately associated (about r .38). 'Children read behaviour far more accurately than they absorb instruction' is a fabricated comparative. It is also a near-duplicate of SF-TRV-000011.
Relative-effort point is correct, genuinely teaches, and fits the app's intergenerational audience. Distractors are plausible and it avoids any body or capability shaming.

Invents a vivid causal mechanism and marks a mainstream alternative wrong. 'The brain's map of limb length is briefly out of date' is one hypothesis among several (changed moments of inertia — up to ~46% in a year, slower processing, greater reliance on vision, incomplete automatisation), and at least one study found body representation does NOT lag behind the pubertal growth spurt. Meanwhile the option marked wrong, 'bones grow before muscles do', is a standard textbook explanation. Stated as 'simplified' with no acknowledgement the mechanism is argued over.

The answer is right and well supported (NSCA/AAP: no detrimental effect on linear growth, no documented growth-plate fractures under competent instruction), which is exactly why this belongs at confidence 'established' with a source rather than sourceless 'simplified' — it is a strength-training recommendation for children. The origin story is also unsupported: 'smaller children were once more likely to be put in weightlifting' is asserted as the cause of the myth when the usual attribution is old child-labour and case-report data. Add a source, soften the origin claim.
Faster between-bout recovery in children versus adults is well supported, and the item correctly declines the easier and wronger claim that children simply have more stamina.

Gradual decline plus responsiveness to training is correct and matches the falls-prevention evidence. Correct option is not the longest, and 'a great deal' is a defensible intensifier given the size of balance-training effects.
Stroke volume is the right primary answer, and the explanation correctly kills two real misconceptions (lungs growing, needing less oxygen) rather than restating the option.
Correct, and it hands the reader something they can actually verify on themselves in two months, which is the best kind of item here. Correct option is the shortest.
Safe and correct triage guidance, with the ordinary-vs-warning distinction drawn cleanly and no diagnosis offered. Content overlaps SF-TRV-000015 closely enough that the pool should keep only one.

Test-craft: the three distractors are all self-evidently bad advice (push through, repeat the thing that hurt, rest until zero sensation), so the answer is pickable by elimination with no knowledge. Content: 'Complete rest is rarely needed and often slows things down' is stated as settled fact with no source, and the item never distinguishes ordinary next-day muscle soreness from pain that is a reason to stop — a 9-year-old with a genuine injury is told to train gentler today.

Contested advice labelled simplified. 'Drink before you're thirsty' is the older ACSM-style line; the Third International Exercise-Associated Hyponatremia Consensus and the Wilderness Medical Society guidelines now recommend drinking to thirst specifically because pre-emptive drinking drives overdrinking. The explanation states 'Thirst lags behind what you've actually lost' as established. Test-craft: the correct option is the longest and the only non-absurd one — the other three (go harder in heat, skip drinking, wear more layers) are joke distractors.

The core (cold water shock gasp reflex) is right, but the explanation asserts the danger is 'not the temperature or how long you stay' — that is false. Swim failure within minutes and hypothermia later are real, documented cold-water killers, and telling a child duration doesn't matter is the wrong takeaway from a drowning-safety item. Also, a safety claim of this weight is carried with sources: [] and the advice 'getting in slowly' implicitly endorses entering cold open water rather than the standard float-and-don't-enter guidance.

Safe, teaches the scaling principle with concrete substitutions, and distractor 0 ('wait until it has cleared up') is a genuinely plausible choice rather than a straw man. No factual claim to over-firm.

Test-craft only; the content is correct. The right answer is the longest and most specific option, one distractor is a bare dismissal ('Nothing — it's a different movement') which the rubric names explicitly, and another ('it's harder, because your feet have less grip') is not plausible. Answerable without knowing the fact.

Genuinely contested, labelled simplified, and stated firmly: 'it's the getting up that shows in the measurements' and 'a single evening session doesn't replace' it. Acute metabolic studies support sitting breaks, but the Ekelund harmonised meta-analysis (>1M people) found high MVPA largely eliminated the mortality risk of high sitting time — whether breaks matter independently of exercise is exactly the open question. Text must say the question is open. Distractor 0 is also a bare dismissal ('Nothing much — it can't be helped').

Two firmness defects. (1) 'people blink roughly half as often while reading a screen' — the controlled screen-vs-hard-copy studies found no significant blink-rate difference (14.9 vs 13.6/min); the halving figure comes from comparing screens to relaxed rest, and the driver is cognitive demand, not the screen. (2) 'The screen isn't damaging anything' is a flat reassurance to children that runs against current myopia evidence, where prolonged near work and screen time in children are repeatedly associated with myopia risk. Also 'holds one muscle still' misdescribes accommodation — the ciliary muscle is sustainedly contracted, not still.

Predictive/feedforward interception is well supported, the distractors are all plausible mechanisms, the correct option is not the longest, and the explanation genuinely explains rather than restating.

Accurate — skill automation shifts control to circuits that run without attention, and muscles store no motor program. The spinal-cord distractor is a strong plausible wrong answer, and the item corrects a real folk belief instead of just naming it.

Gluteus maximus is the largest single muscle by volume and mass; the thigh distractor is a defensible-sounding alternative and the explanation names why the quadriceps feels like the answer. Correct at the stated simplified level.
Correct, options are evenly weighted single terms with no length or specificity tell, and the Achilles-as-largest-tendon detail is accurate and gives the reader something to feel on their own body.
Correct, balanced short options, and the explanation earns its place by contrasting ligament with tendon rather than restating the answer.
206 is standard, and the item is unusually careful for a number item — it says roughly, explains the fusion from ~300 infant bones, and notes real individual variation.

Arithmetic checks out (27 per hand, 26 per foot = 106 of ~206), 'more than half' is correctly hedged as more-than rather than a fake precise share, and the explanation actively corrects the half-remembered 'quarter in your feet' version.

Bone remodelling is continuous at every age; loading-driven thickening and disuse thinning are both correct. Options are comparable in length and the distractors are real misconceptions rather than jokes.
Correct on marrow and haematopoiesis, and the honeycomb-not-hollow line pre-empts the obvious wrong inference. No over-firm quantities.

The cartilage-plus-synovial-fluid answer and the slicker-than-ice comparison are sound, but the closing clause invents a causal mechanism beyond the evidence: 'the fluid spreads better the more you move, which is why joints feel easier a few minutes into a walk.' Why early-walk stiffness eases is not established as synovial fluid distribution — that is textbook folklore. Cut the causal claim or mark it as one idea among several.

Elbow as hinge is the right simplification at this level, and the explanation correctly attributes forearm rotation to the radius crossing the ulna rather than to the hinge — it heads off the obvious misconception.
Correct, and the explanation is accurate on all three wrong options (knee hinge with some rotation, jaw hinge that also translates), so the distractors teach as well as the answer.
'Muscles can only pull' is the rubric's own example of a sound simplification, and the bicep/tricep pairing makes the consequence concrete. Options are evenly weighted.
Stapes is ~3mm and is the last of the three ossicles; the grain-of-rice comparison is fair. Options are balanced and none is longer or more specific than the rest.
Femur is the longest bone and averages about a quarter of stature; 'roughly' is the correct amount of hedging for a figure that varies between people. The measure-a-friend hook is age-appropriate.
Pulmonary circulation is correctly described, and the two-pumps-one-organ framing plus the thicker left wall is a real insight rather than a restatement.
Gas exchange correct; the alveolar membrane is genuinely far thinner than tissue paper, so the comparison is earned. Sugar and salt distractors are plausible and are addressed in the explanation.

Correct — the pulse is the pressure wave, and pulse wave velocity does greatly exceed blood flow velocity, so 'far faster' is an earned comparative. The heart-felt-through-skin distractor is the actual common misconception.

'Lungs contain no muscle at all' is false — the airways inside the lungs are wrapped in smooth muscle, which is precisely what constricts in asthma. For an app used by nine-year-olds, some of whom have inhalers, that is the wrong sentence to state absolutely; the intended point is that lungs contain no muscle that pumps air. Test-craft: the correct option is also the longest and the only one carrying an anatomical descriptor.

About one minute at rest is consistent with ~5 L blood volume and ~5 L/min cardiac output, and the exercise comparison is correctly left qualitative ('considerably quicker') rather than given a fake number.

Correctly labelled contested and, unusually, the text says so in plain language — the control of exercise hyperpnoea genuinely remains unresolved. The answer itself is right, the distractors are plausible (panting-to-shed-heat especially), and the correct option is not the longest.
Accurate on the cardiac notch and the 2-vs-3 lobe asymmetry, and the 'they take turns' distractor is a real misconception. Explicitly corrects it ('Both work all the time').
Correct, and it kills the blue-blood myth properly by naming the actual cause (skin optics) rather than just denying it. All four options are plausible-sounding versions of the myth.

Handled with the right firmness for a figure that is genuinely uncertain: the option and the explanation both say 'estimates' and give an order of magnitude rather than the often-repeated precise 60,000 miles.
Correct, and the explanation supplies the reason the narrowness matters (exchange requires cells close to the wall) instead of restating the definition.
Venous valves and the calf muscle pump are correct, and the point about the heart's push being nearly spent by that stage is the part that actually explains why valves are needed.
Etymology correct. The trailing 'a sprint-and-stop game counts differently' is vague, but it is not a factual claim and the item is otherwise sound.

Unearned comparative plus a contested area labelled simplified. 'Bodies cope with variety far better than with any single position held for hours' is a firm magnitude nobody measured, and posture's relationship to pain is genuinely argued over — the item presents the physio saying as settled. State the variety point without 'far better', or mark the question as open.

Counter-rotating arm swing and its metabolic benefit are supported (held arms measurably increase walking cost), and 'measurably cheaper' is the correct level of firmness — a direction, not an invented percentage.

The anti-movement/stabilising role of the core is mainstream, hedged correctly with 'mostly', and the one-handed shopping example makes it usable. No body-composition or aesthetic framing, which this topic often attracts.

The answer (shorter steps need less utilised friction) is right, but the explanation's mechanism is muddled and over-stated: 'A long stride pushes you forward and backward as much as up' is an unmeasured quantitative claim, and it then calls that same forward/backward force 'sideways', which will confuse a nine-year-old. Test-craft: the correct option is the longest by a clear margin and the only one offering a physical mechanism.
True, useful, and framed as capability across a lifespan rather than as fixing a body. Options are single words with no tell.
Definitional and correct; the strength and flexibility distractors are the common confusions, and the catching example separates timing from power in one line.

Lever-arm reasoning is correct and the four options are parallel in form and length with no tell. The reframing of 'lift with your legs' is a reasonable inference from the biomechanics rather than an invented mechanism.

Diurnal foot swelling is well documented and is the standard reason for the afternoon shoe-fitting advice. The correct option is the shortest, so there is no length tell, and the claim is kept to 'slightly'.

Unearned superlative: 'It's the single biggest cause of next-day soreness in ordinary walking' is a ranking nobody has measured. The eccentric-contraction core is correct and worth keeping — 'a major cause' would be defensible, 'the single biggest' is not. Test-craft: the correct option is also the longest and the only mechanistic one.

The content is correct and well chosen, but the explanation instructs the reader to close their eyes and move ('Close your eyes and touch your nose'). The rubric's safety list bans eyes-closed movement without qualification, and this ships to seniors as well as children. Trivially fixable — 'without looking' does the same job.

Pickable without knowing the fact: the correct option is the longest and the only inclusive one, while all three distractors announce their own weakness with 'alone' or 'on its own'. The explanation also invents a mechanism — 'Three sources vote, and your brain goes with the majority' — where the actual process is weighted sensory integration, not majority rule, and it reduces the whole somatosensory channel to 'pressure sensors in your feet'.
Sensorimotor adaptation to ship motion and the readaptation on land are well described; the claim is hedged at the right level and teaches a real mechanism.

"in a way standing still never can" is an absolute nobody measured, and the underlying claim that carrying a tray trains balance is asserted, not evidenced. Drop the absolute and state it as a plausible difference in demand, not a training effect.

Safety: a single-leg stand at a bathroom sink, on a hard and often wet floor, is suggested to an audience that includes seniors, with no mention of keeping a hand near the counter and no naming of the fall risk. Also frames it as "two minutes of practice" when nobody balances on one foot for the full two minutes.
Postural control continues maturing well past toddlerhood into adolescence. True, correctly unquantified, and useful for a young reader.
Symmetric loading keeps the centre of mass closer to the base of support; a one-sided load forces trunk compensation. True at this level of detail, no overclaim.
Plantar cutaneous feedback is a genuine contributor to postural control, and the item hedges honestly ("part of why", "feels steadier") rather than claiming barefoot is measurably better.
Age-related decline in balance is well established; the second clause is an explicit value judgement about spending a minute, not a dose or sufficiency claim.
Single-support phase of gait is real and this reframes something familiar without overstating it.

Firmness. "Most of the tightness" is a proportion nobody measured, and the mechanism is actively argued: current reviews find both reduced passive stiffness and increased stretch tolerance contribute, with tolerance dominant only over longer training periods. Either hedge ("a lot of what you feel is...") or mark contested and say the question is open.

Two defects. It opens with "That's why", a dangling referent to SF-FCT-000190 that breaks when the item is served on its own, which is how this library is read. And "your body has decided the position is safe" is a vivid causal mechanism stated as fact for an acute effect whose cause is not settled.
Hamstrings are biarticular and hip/knee position genuinely changes what a forward bend loads. Accurate and explanatory.

"a lot of why" is an unmeasured proportion, and "shortened position" is the weakest-supported version of this claim. Evidence supports increased passive hip-flexor stiffness and reduced hip extension after prolonged sitting, not structural shortening; no study links length of sitting to hip flexor tightness directly. Rewrite as stiffness, and drop the proportion.
Correct contrast between a multiaxial and a uniaxial joint, and the "on purpose" framing teaches the trade-off rather than just naming parts.
The glenohumeral joint being the most mobile joint in the body is standard anatomy, and the mobility/stability trade-off is correctly stated.

Both halves are wrong in a safety-relevant direction. Ballistic stretching is discouraged primarily for injury risk, not merely because it is "less controlled", and the item explicitly downplays that. And "the range you gain looks much the same either way" is contradicted: meta-analytic comparisons put ballistic stretching's effect on range of motion below static and PNF. Telling a nine-year-old that bouncing gets the same result is the opposite of the guideline.
Individual variation in connective tissue and joint laxity is real, and "some people" keeps it appropriately unquantified. Also usefully defuses comparison between bodies.

The exhale-lets-you-sink-further claim is gym folklore stated as fact ("usually"), with no good evidence behind it, and "Holding your breath does the opposite" invents a matching effect. It also introduces breath-holding as a technique to a nine-year-old audience, which the safety rules avoid. Cut the breath-holding half or reframe the whole item as relaxation, not range.
reviewer accepted, but measured claim 'better than' with no sources — a comparative, proportion or dose needs one whatever the confidence tier says; hedge it or cite it
Distinguishing stretch tension from sharp pain is exactly the right safety cue for this audience, and it is stated without diagnosing anything.
Accurate description of segmental spinal motion summing to gross range. Teaches something a reader will not have pictured.
Verified: the Achilles is described in the anatomical literature as the thickest and strongest tendon in the body, formed from gastrocnemius and soleus and inserting on the calcaneus.
Pandiculation is a real, widely observed vertebrate behaviour and naming it is worth the reader's attention. The "old enough to have its own name" line is a loose flourish but makes no health claim.
Latissimus dorsi runs from the humerus to the thoracolumbar fascia and lower spine, so an overhead reach does load far more than the arm. Accurate.
Accurate description of psoas major, correctly left unnamed for a nine-year-old, and the length of the muscle is genuinely surprising.

"almost nothing" is an overstatement and it contradicts SF-FCT-000197 in this same packet: generalised connective-tissue laxity is precisely why hypermobility is scored across multiple joints. Joint specificity is real; the strength of the claim is not. Soften to "tell you less than you would think".

"the same mechanism" is an unearned identity claim between two practices that have not been shown to work identically, and what follows the colon is a description of practice (regular time at end range), not a mechanism. Restate as "work the same way in practice" or cut the mechanism framing.

Quality failure. It restates SF-FCT-000203 with the content removed and teaches nothing checkable; "one your body asked for on its own" is a phrase, not a fact. Either fold into the pandiculation item or give it real content.

Anatomically wrong: the ankle (talocrural) joint is classified as a uniaxial hinge, the same category as the knee and elbow; the side-to-side motion comes from the subtalar joint below it. "universal joints" is also not a standard classification for the wrist, which is condyloid. And "can't possibly suit all of them" is an overclaim on top of the error.

Stated more firmly than the neuroscience supports. The clean prefrontal-to-striatum handoff is the old account; current work finds both systems remain active and compete rather than one replacing the other, and cortical involvement is task-dependent. "stops needing willpower" also overstates automaticity. Should be hedged or marked contested.

Two proportions nobody measured: "nearly always" and "Most people feel better a few minutes in". There is real work on people mispredicting how exercise will feel, but not at this firmness. Label editorial or hedge to "often".

An absolute and a superlative in one sentence. "Every habit needs a cue" is stated as a law, and "the most reliable cue is" ranks cue types against each other on no measurement — existing-routine anchoring is supported as effective, not as most reliable.
Implementation intentions are among the better-replicated findings in this area, and "noticeably more likely" is hedged correctly rather than quoting an effect size the item cannot source.

"beats" is a head-to-head comparative between two approaches that have not been compared head to head. It is also advice, not a simplified fact, so the confidence label is wrong — SF-FCT-000220 shows `editorial` is available and unused here.

Misstates the peak-end rule: it is peak AND end that dominate retrospective evaluation, and this item drops the peak entirely. "is what pulls you back" then asserts a single cause for return behaviour that the evidence supports only as one predictor among several.

"far more" is an unmeasured comparative. The defensible version — missing a single day does not derail habit formation — is worth saying, but not with a magnitude attached, and this is editorial rather than simplified.

"Streaks work because" asserts a mechanism for the app's own core feature with nothing behind it, and picks one explanation (visibility) over the more obvious ones (loss aversion, commitment). Either hedge to "part of why streaks work" or mark it editorial and own it as a product opinion.

The reactivity of self-monitoring is a real effect, but "purely because you're now paying attention to it" is a mechanism overclaim — tracking also changes what people choose to do because they know it will be recorded. Drop "purely".

"usually physical" is an unmeasured proportion and is likely wrong: the barriers people report most are time, fatigue and how they expect it to feel, not where the shoes are. The examples are good; the ranking claim is not earned.
reviewer accepted, but measured claim 'Most people' with no sources — a comparative, proportion or dose needs one whatever the confidence tier says; hedge it or cite it
"holds up better" is presented as a finding but is a comparative nobody measured. Cue consistency is supported in general; time-of-day versus mood specifically is not. Hedge or relabel editorial.
Plainly advice in advice voice, sound, safe, and consistent with the implementation-intention literature without claiming to be a measurement.
Reward immediacy is a well-supported principle of learning, and "stick best" here refers to a genuine and large timing effect rather than an invented ranking.

"The clearest sign" is an unearned superlative. Reduced conscious deliberation and a sense of oddity when skipping are indicators of automaticity, but nothing establishes this as the clearest one. "A good sign" fixes it.
A clean, safe framing that moves attention from outcome goals to today's action, with no empirical claim to overstate.
"faster than changing your mind does" is a speed comparison between two things never measured against each other. The environment-shapes-behaviour point survives without the race.

Planning fallacy, correctly stated including the direction of the error (people overestimate what they will finish). Hedged with 'reliably poor' rather than a made-up percentage. Age-appropriate and useful.

Small-dose habit framing is consistent with the app's values and safe; the second clause (repetition ingrains whatever pattern is repeated) is ordinary motor-learning and is stated without a fake number. Teaches something real about form.

Firmness defect. 'is what keeps MOST streaks alive' is an unearned proportion — nobody measured what keeps most streaks alive. The underlying idea (implementation intentions / if-then plans help adherence) is supported, but it is stated as a measured majority. Soften to something like 'Deciding in advance what you'll do on the day you don't feel like it is one of the things that keeps a streak alive.'

Two unearned comparatives in one item: 'Kids move most when nobody calls it exercise' (superlative) and 'tends to go on considerably longer' (a quantified duration comparison nobody measured here). The core observation — framing activity as play rather than exercise raises engagement — is plausible but is stated far more firmly than any cited evidence. Also `simplified` with no source for what is really a behavioural research claim.
Hedged ('most children', 'given time, space, and no instructions'), safe, and true of free play at the level of detail given. The closing line is editorial colour rather than a factual overreach.
Properly hedged with 'often'. Side-by-side walking reducing the pressure of a hard conversation is a modest, non-medical claim and is not stated as a measured effect. Safe for all ages.
Household behaviour concordance is real and the item hedges twice ('usually', 'a little'). No mechanism is invented and no proportion is claimed.
Sibling modelling is well documented, and the claim is hedged with 'tend to'. The 'coaches' line is framing, not an invented effect. Safe and age-appropriate.

Stated as a guaranteed outcome: a weekly repeat 'turns it into a landmark that kids still remember years later.' Family-ritual research supports that rituals are valued and remembered, but not that repeating anything weekly reliably produces a decades-long memory. Needs a hedge ('can become', 'often') rather than a promise.
'far more likely' is an unearned magnitude. Choice/autonomy does support intrinsic motivation, but the size of the effect here is invented. Drop 'far' or cite the autonomy-support evidence.
Straightforwardly true (incidental daily activity is real movement), no number claimed, safe, and it usefully reframes existing activity without any body or weight framing.

Safety. The item invites a nine-year-old to race 'to the end of the street' and does not name the traffic hazard, which the rubric requires for anything a child could copy and be hurt by. Relocate it to a safe setting (park, yard, path) or name the condition explicitly.
Warm, safe, non-comparative, and makes a genuine point about modelling across generations. No factual claim to overreach on.
reviewer accepted, but measured claim 'better than' with no sources — a comparative, proportion or dose needs one whatever the confidence tier says; hedge it or cite it
True, safe, and it reframes chores as movement without any weight or body-composition framing. Modest but it does teach the reframe.

Hedged with 'usually' and framed against adult expectation rather than as a measurement. Children being more fatigue-resistant in intermittent play is well supported, and the boredom half is plainly observational.
Inclusive, safe, no comparison of bodies, and it makes a real point about pacing a group. Nothing to verify and nothing overstated.

'one of the few things' is an unearned superlative and is easy to falsify — a nine-year-old and a sixty-year-old can genuinely cook, play games, garden or make music side by side too. The point survives without the ranking: say movement is one of the things they can do side by side at their own speeds.
Hedged with 'often', and the accountability/telling-someone effect is a reasonable, non-medical claim. No proportion or magnitude invented.

Three firmness problems stacked: 'the MOST reliable exercise partners', 'in MOST households', and the causal 'mainly because'. None of that is measured, and the dog-walking literature is actually mixed — a large share of dog owners do not walk their dog regularly. Rewrite as an observation about the daily prompt a dog provides, without the superlative or the household proportion.
True and non-quantified: playground play does develop balance, coordination and confidence. Safe, and the closing point (it doesn't feel like training) is the actual insight.
Correctly labelled `editorial`, which licenses the firmness of 'is the one that sticks'. Safe, no medical claim, and it says something worth reading to an adult user.
Hedged with 'tend to' on both halves and framed as a comparison against adults' own expectations rather than a measured quantity. Consistent with modelling research.

Verified anatomy: the fingers contain no muscle bellies; flexion and extension come from extrinsic forearm muscles acting through long tendons. The puppet-string image is an accurate simplification, not an invented mechanism.
Verified: 26 bones per foot, 52 of roughly 206 bones, which is genuinely about a quarter. The proportion is one of the few in this packet that is actually arithmetic rather than assertion.
Verified: the malleus, incus and stapes are the smallest bones in the body, the largest about 8 mm. 'All three on a fingernail' is a fair size image, not an invented measurement.

Verified: the femur is the longest and strongest bone, and its anterior bow (a real, named feature) is correctly described as a slight curve rather than straight. Good detail that most readers won't know.

Verified on both halves: the function of yawning genuinely is unresolved (and the item says so, which is the honest handling of an open question), and reading or thinking about yawning is a documented contagion trigger. 'Often' is the right hedge.
reviewer accepted, but measured claim 'more than' with no sources — a comparative, proportion or dose needs one whatever the confidence tier says; hedge it or cite it
Microsaccades and fixational drift are established and the item claims nothing beyond their existence and imperceptibility. Genuinely surprising to a reader, which is what this category is for.

Verified: two lobes on the left, three on the right, and the left lung's cardiac notch really is the heart occupying that space. The 'gave up a lobe's worth of space' phrasing is a simplification of standard anatomy, not an invented mechanism.

'About a minute' is the mainstream resting figure (roughly 5 L blood over roughly 5 L/min cardiac output); published estimates run 20-60 seconds, so 'about a minute' is within range and appropriately approximate.

'Tens of thousands of miles' is the correctly loose version of the commonly cited 60,000-mile estimate — notably, the item did NOT commit to the precise figure, which is the right call given the estimate's softness.
reviewer accepted, but measured claim 'faster than' with no sources — a comparative, proportion or dose needs one whatever the confidence tier says; hedge it or cite it
Established bone biology — vascularised, innervated, continuously remodelled — stated without any dose, rate or proportion. Corrects a real misconception children hold.
Verified: the auricular muscles are present in everyone and voluntary control is variable. Stated with the correct hedge ('only some people'), no proportion invented.
Verified and non-obvious: the visible lingual papillae are not themselves taste buds; the buds sit in the epithelium along the papillae's walls. A genuine correction of a common misconception.
reviewer accepted, but measured claim 'most of' with no sources — a comparative, proportion or dose needs one whatever the confidence tier says; hedge it or cite it
'About a fifth' matches the standard ~20% of resting metabolic rate for the brain, and the 'even when sitting still' clause is the correct and interesting part.

Verified against NASA: spinal lengthening in microgravity is commonly cited as up to about 3%, roughly two inches for a tall adult, so 'an inch or two' is accurate. The item also actively corrects the 'no gravity in space' misconception with the right explanation (free fall), which is a bonus rather than a defect.

Firmness defect of exactly the type this library has. The first half (fingernails grow faster than toenails) is solidly established; the second half — 'the nails on your dominant hand grow fastest of all' — is stated flatly as fact when the evidence is mixed: it rests largely on Bean's decades-long self-observation, and at least one peer-reviewed comparison found no significant right/left difference. Either drop the dominant-hand clause or mark it as something people have noticed but not settled.
Safe, non-clinical resilience framing that explicitly refuses to tell a reader they shouldn't find hard things hard. No mechanism, dose or proportion claimed.

'the one that changes the most' is an unearned superlative, ranking sleep above every other self-care behaviour with nothing to support the ranking. Sleep's importance is not in doubt; the league table is. Rewrite without the ranking, e.g. 'and one of the ones that changes the most.'
Safe, age-appropriate conflict guidance with no medical or psychological claim beyond common sense. Nothing to overstate.

Defines gratitude honestly and explicitly rules out toxic positivity ('isn't pretending things are fine'), which is the right handling for a young audience. No claim about outcomes or benefits, so nothing to overreach.
Editorial, correctly labelled, safe, non-shaming, and useful to a 9-year-old. No factual claim to overstate.
Correctly hedged ('is linked to'), and 'short counts' is supported by the physical-activity/mood literature. Simplified label is honest here.

'Most people are far harsher with themselves than they would ever be out loud' states a measured-sounding proportion and comparative that nobody has measured. The advice is fine; soften to 'many people' or drop the quantifier.

The answer key is contradicted by the evidence it leans on. Meta-analysis puts parental modelling at a weak association with child activity (summary r about .16) while parental support and encouragement is moderate (about .38) — i.e. the option marked wrong ('being told regularly that exercise matters') is, if anything, the better-supported one. 'Children copy what adults do far more reliably than they follow what they're told' is an unearned comparative pointing the wrong way. Also duplicates SF-TRV-000025.

Two problems. Firmness: 'rehearsal likes frequency more than duration' is a comparative presented as settled; frequency-vs-duration for balance training has not been cleanly separated.

Content is good (specific compressive strength vs overall strength is the right debunk). Rebuild the distractors.

10-20 minute nap guidance and the sleep-inertia explanation are correct, the correct option is not the longest, and the distractors are all real beliefs. 'Without much cost to that night' is doing a little work unqualified but stays inside simplified for a short nap.

'Reliably takes some of the heat out of it' is stated more firmly than the evidence supports. Affect labelling has mixed results, unclear mechanisms, and findings that it can interfere with subsequent reappraisal; short-term effects are often null. This is closer to contested than simplified, and the text does not say the question is open. Soften to 'often' and drop 'reliably'.

The correct option is phenomenological (writing forces sequence) rather than an efficacy claim, and the explanation explicitly refuses to claim it solves anything. Correct option is the longest, which is a mild tell, but the distractors are genuine beliefs about journalling.

Definitional rather than an efficacy claim, which is the right call given how contested growth-mindset intervention effects are. The explanation actively heads off the 'you can be anything' inflation, and the correct option is the shortest.
Arousal-reappraisal framing is well supported, safe, and genuinely useful at min_age 9. Distractors are the beliefs a nervous child actually holds.
Vigilance decrement is well established, including that it occurs within tens of minutes and independently of felt tiredness, and brief-break restoration is reasonable at simplified level.

Unearned ranking: 'Enjoyment predicts whether someone is still moving years later better than talent, early starts or encouragement do' is a head-to-head comparison nobody has run, and the encouragement leg is doubtful — parental support/encouragement shows a moderate association with child activity in meta-analysis. Keep the enjoyment claim, drop the league table.

Safe, on-message, and the explanation does real work (comparison changes the subject from 'did I move' to 'am I winning'). 'It works on everyone' is a small over-reach but the claim is a values statement, not a measurement.

The question demands a proportion nobody has measured, and the answer it awards ('Most of it') points against the evidence: parental modelling is weakly associated with child activity (about r .16) while parental support and instruction is moderately associated (about r .38). 'Children read behaviour far more accurately than they absorb instruction' is a fabricated comparative. It is also a near-duplicate of SF-TRV-000011.
Relative-effort point is correct, genuinely teaches, and fits the app's intergenerational audience. Distractors are plausible and it avoids any body or capability shaming.

Invents a vivid causal mechanism and marks a mainstream alternative wrong. 'The brain's map of limb length is briefly out of date' is one hypothesis among several (changed moments of inertia — up to ~46% in a year, slower processing, greater reliance on vision, incomplete automatisation), and at least one study found body representation does NOT lag behind the pubertal growth spurt. Meanwhile the option marked wrong, 'bones grow before muscles do', is a standard textbook explanation. Stated as 'simplified' with no acknowledgement the mechanism is argued over.

The answer is right and well supported (NSCA/AAP: no detrimental effect on linear growth, no documented growth-plate fractures under competent instruction), which is exactly why this belongs at confidence 'established' with a source rather than sourceless 'simplified' — it is a strength-training recommendation for children. The origin story is also unsupported: 'smaller children were once more likely to be put in weightlifting' is asserted as the cause of the myth when the usual attribution is old child-labour and case-report data. Add a source, soften the origin claim.
Faster between-bout recovery in children versus adults is well supported, and the item correctly declines the easier and wronger claim that children simply have more stamina.

Gradual decline plus responsiveness to training is correct and matches the falls-prevention evidence. Correct option is not the longest, and 'a great deal' is a defensible intensifier given the size of balance-training effects.
Stroke volume is the right primary answer, and the explanation correctly kills two real misconceptions (lungs growing, needing less oxygen) rather than restating the option.
Correct, and it hands the reader something they can actually verify on themselves in two months, which is the best kind of item here. Correct option is the shortest.

Test-craft: the three distractors are all self-evidently bad advice (push through, repeat the thing that hurt, rest until zero sensation), so the answer is pickable by elimination with no knowledge. Content: 'Complete rest is rarely needed and often slows things down' is stated as settled fact with no source, and the item never distinguishes ordinary next-day muscle soreness from pain that is a reason to stop — a 9-year-old with a genuine injury is told to train gentler today.

Contested advice labelled simplified. 'Drink before you're thirsty' is the older ACSM-style line; the Third International Exercise-Associated Hyponatremia Consensus and the Wilderness Medical Society guidelines now recommend drinking to thirst specifically because pre-emptive drinking drives overdrinking. The explanation states 'Thirst lags behind what you've actually lost' as established. Test-craft: the correct option is the longest and the only non-absurd one — the other three (go harder in heat, skip drinking, wear more layers) are joke distractors.

The core (cold water shock gasp reflex) is right, but the explanation asserts the danger is 'not the temperature or how long you stay' — that is false. Swim failure within minutes and hypothermia later are real, documented cold-water killers, and telling a child duration doesn't matter is the wrong takeaway from a drowning-safety item. Also, a safety claim of this weight is carried with sources: [] and the advice 'getting in slowly' implicitly endorses entering cold open water rather than the standard float-and-don't-enter guidance.

Safe, teaches the scaling principle with concrete substitutions, and distractor 0 ('wait until it has cleared up') is a genuinely plausible choice rather than a straw man. No factual claim to over-firm.

Test-craft only; the content is correct. The right answer is the longest and most specific option, one distractor is a bare dismissal ('Nothing — it's a different movement') which the rubric names explicitly, and another ('it's harder, because your feet have less grip') is not plausible. Answerable without knowing the fact.

Genuinely contested, labelled simplified, and stated firmly: 'it's the getting up that shows in the measurements' and 'a single evening session doesn't replace' it. Acute metabolic studies support sitting breaks, but the Ekelund harmonised meta-analysis (>1M people) found high MVPA largely eliminated the mortality risk of high sitting time — whether breaks matter independently of exercise is exactly the open question. Text must say the question is open. Distractor 0 is also a bare dismissal ('Nothing much — it can't be helped').

Two firmness defects. (1) 'people blink roughly half as often while reading a screen' — the controlled screen-vs-hard-copy studies found no significant blink-rate difference (14.9 vs 13.6/min); the halving figure comes from comparing screens to relaxed rest, and the driver is cognitive demand, not the screen. (2) 'The screen isn't damaging anything' is a flat reassurance to children that runs against current myopia evidence, where prolonged near work and screen time in children are repeatedly associated with myopia risk. Also 'holds one muscle still' misdescribes accommodation — the ciliary muscle is sustainedly contracted, not still.
reviewer accepted, but measured claim 'harder than' with no sources — a comparative, proportion or dose needs one whatever the confidence tier says; hedge it or cite it

Accurate — skill automation shifts control to circuits that run without attention, and muscles store no motor program. The spinal-cord distractor is a strong plausible wrong answer, and the item corrects a real folk belief instead of just naming it.

Correct on marrow and haematopoiesis, and the honeycomb-not-hollow line pre-empts the obvious wrong inference. No over-firm quantities.

Pulmonary circulation is correctly described, and the two-pumps-one-organ framing plus the thicker left wall is a real insight rather than a restatement.

'Lungs contain no muscle at all' is false — the airways inside the lungs are wrapped in smooth muscle, which is precisely what constricts in asthma. For an app used by nine-year-olds, some of whom have inhalers, that is the wrong sentence to state absolutely; the intended point is that lungs contain no muscle that pumps air. Test-craft: the correct option is also the longest and the only one carrying an anatomical descriptor.

Pickable without knowing the fact: the correct option is the longest and the only inclusive one, while all three distractors announce their own weakness with 'alone' or 'on its own'. recommends eyes-closed single-leg balance as a way to make the exercise harder ('such a good way to make the exercise harder without moving anything').
